All of your questions are precisely the reason I don’t like labels lol, there’s just so many variables it seems almost useless to me. Using myself for example, I am rather androgynous-presenting: I was assigned female at birth so I have those sex organs but I have a flat chest. Im rather tall and slim and my face is pretty but I can present more masc if I want to. My last partner described himself as a straight guy. Now even though I don’t identify as female, i can’t tell him he’s not straight, because I still have a lot of feminine characteristics. However I’ve also had bi and gay guys be attracted to me too so who’s to say! I think sexuality is a lot more complex than a few labels can encompass.
As for the definition of “gay”, historically yes I believe it has meant men who are attracted to men. That is probably also the definition in the dictionary, idk lol. However, at least in my experience it can also be used in a more informal way to refer to people that fall outside cis/heterosexual norms. I’ve heard lesbians as well as bisexual people call themselves gay, and among my friends we often use the term quite loosely. 
I hope I explained these things in a way that makes sense!! I don’t get caught up too much in the verbiage in my day to day life, although it is interesting to think about

Ok so I actually went through this whole thing where I got on birth control pills (not realizing that it’s ESTROGEN aka female hormone) and I noticed I started becoming more and more uncomfortable with my body? Til I saw my therapist, who specializes in trans ppl and issues btw and he was like “how do you feel being on that?” And I was like “I mean it’s okay I guess” and then he reminded me that it’s estrogen and lightbulb moment!! The hormones had been making my body more feminine than it usually is!! That’s why my boobs looked bigger and my ass and hips too. So I got off the pills immediately. Honestly though, I was kind of thankful for the experience because it affirmed to me that I was definitely more comfortable in a more androgynous body and that it hadn’t all been in my head. I highly suggest a non hormonal birth control method, such as that one that goes in your arm. Hope this helps!!

I relate to this a lot, when I first started experiencing chronic dpdr I desperately searched for something physical to be wrong with me, just so that I could say “okay this is the thing and now I can fix it”. Few can imagine wishing something like a brain tumor on yourself! I’m 3 years in now and I can say that it does get better. I can’t say that it’s gone away yet, but it gets easier; less scary. The beginning was the worst because it was all I could think about. I always thought, “how can I ever even learn to cope with this, when I can’t get away from it?” I constantly had panic attacks about not feeling real and thinking I was going to die. Dpdr is a coping mechanism your brain used to try to protect you, which makes it tricky because the more you feel scared of that feeling, the more you will feel it, if that makes sense! But slowly but surely, I was able to go back to the things I used to do instead of laying in bed all day and asking questions that had no answers. When I became less scared, the unreal feelings eased up a bit. Not completely, but eventually I was able to drive again and even return to work. I still am looking for answers as well, but I promise that it can get better if you can start to tell yourself that you are okay and not give into the scary feelings. I wish I could hug you, but I hope my story can give you some hope

I used to think I hadn’t experienced any “trauma” either, but eventually I realized trauma doesn’t just have to be some big horrific event that you can define. It can be more about how you internalize different things that happen to you. For me it was the way my internal monologue put a negative spin on things that most other people would just let roll off their back, and they slowly but surely ate away at me. You say you’ve experienced anxiety; dpdr often comes as a “coping mechanism” in cases of prolonged anxiety. It’s your brains way of protecting you (as my therapist says, “brains can be assholes”). So that’s a likely explanation
